title: Remove Nth Node From End
description: Remove the n-th node from the end in a single pass. Two pointers: fast moves n steps ahead, then both advance until fast hits null — slow lands on the node BEFORE the one to remove.

conversation.intro: How an interview about this problem would actually play out. Each section has two parts: what you'd actually say out loud, and why that move matters. Tap a section to expand.

sections.title: 1. Restate & clarify
sections.prompt: Before touching code — pin down the inputs.
sections.say:
"Let me make sure I have this right: given the head of a singly linked list and a positive integer n, I need to remove the n-th node from the END of the list and return the new head. So for [1,2,3,4,5] with n=2, the second-to-last node is 4, and the result is [1,2,3,5]."

Then a few quick clarifying questions:
• Is n guaranteed to be valid (1 ≤ n ≤ L where L is list length)? Or could n exceed the list length?
• Removing the head — is that possible (i.e., n = L)? Should I handle it gracefully?
• Removing the tail — n = 1?
• Can I make multiple passes through the list, or is single-pass required?
• n is 1-indexed, right? (So n=1 means remove the last node, not the second-to-last.)
sections.why: The single-pass-vs-two-pass question is the load-bearing one. A two-pass solution (count length first, then walk to position L - n) is the obvious answer and is perfectly fine if the interviewer allows it. The single-pass version uses the gap-of-n two-pointer trick. Asking signals you know both exist and lets them pick. The n=L case (remove head) is the edge that justifies introducing a dummy node — without it, you'd need a special case for 'is the head being removed?'.

sections.title: 2. Brute force first (out loud)
sections.prompt: Name the two-pass solution before you optimize.
sections.say:
"The two-pass solution is: walk the list once to count length L. Then walk from the head L - n steps to reach the predecessor of the node to remove. Then unlink with `prev.next = prev.next.next`. Two passes, O(L) time total, O(1) space. Clean, easy to get right, no clever pointer math.

If the interviewer wants a single-pass version, we can replace the two-pass with a two-pointer trick: hold a `fast` pointer n nodes ahead of `slow`, then advance them together until fast hits the end. When fast.next is null, slow is sitting on the predecessor of the target. Same O(L) bound, but one walk through the list instead of two."
sections.why: Two reasons to name the two-pass version out loud. (1) It proves you have a working solution without the trick — interviewers worry about candidates who can ONLY do the clever version. (2) It frames the two-pointer trick as 'do the same work, but interleave the count with the walk' rather than a magic new idea — which it is. The two-pointer gap of n is just 'maintain L - n distance from the end' implicitly via the gap of n from the head.

sections.title: 3. Spot the pattern
sections.prompt: What signal in the problem points to the gap-of-n two-pointer pattern + dummy head?
sections.say:
"This is the canonical 'gap-of-n two pointers' pattern. The structural observation is: 'n-th from the end' is equivalent to 'L - n from the start', and the gap between two pointers separated by n is conserved as they walk. So if I plant `fast` n nodes ahead of `slow`, then advance them in lockstep until `fast` reaches the end, `slow` has walked exactly L - n - 1 nodes from the start — which puts it on the PREDECESSOR of the target. (Predecessor, not target, because I need `slow.next = slow.next.next` to unlink.)

Two specific details. (1) The first loop advances `fast` n times, not n-1 times — get this off by one and you're removing the wrong node. (2) The second loop's condition is `while (fast.next)` not `while (fast)` — that's what makes slow stop at the predecessor instead of the target itself.

And I'll use a dummy head pointing at the original head. That's what lets me handle 'remove the head' (n = L) without a special case: when n = L, fast ends at the original tail, slow ends at dummy, and `slow.next = slow.next.next` cleanly drops the original head. Return `dummy.next`."
sections.why: Naming the pattern AND deriving the loop conditions out loud is what separates this from 'I memorized the code.' The 'gap of n is conserved' framing is the structural insight — once you say it, the two loops fall out: first establish the gap (n iterations advancing fast only), then preserve it while sliding both. The dummy-head detail is what makes 'remove the head' uniform with 'remove any other node' — without it, you'd need a special branch.

sections.title: 4. Trace through examples
sections.prompt: Walk a few inputs to confirm the model before writing the loop.
sections.intro: "Let me trace through a couple of cases to make sure the gap math is right." Three inputs cover the interesting behaviors — a middle-of-list removal, a head-removal that exercises the dummy, and the smallest valid input.

examples.note: Classic case — remove the second-to-last node (4). slow ends at node 3 (the predecessor).
examples.trace:
dummy → 1 → 2 → 3 → 4 → 5
init: fast=dummy, slow=dummy
phase 1 (advance fast n=2 times):
  fast: dummy → 1 → 2
phase 2 (advance both until fast.next is null):
  iter1: fast=3, slow=1
  iter2: fast=4, slow=2
  iter3: fast=5, slow=3. fast.next is null → exit.
unlink: slow=3, slow.next=4, slow.next.next=5. Now 3.next = 5.
return dummy.next → [1,2,3,5]

examples.note: Remove the only node — n equals list length. This is the case the dummy is for.
examples.trace:
dummy → 1
init: fast=dummy, slow=dummy
phase 1 (advance fast n=1 time):
  fast: dummy → 1
phase 2 (advance both until fast.next is null):
  fast=1, fast.next=null → loop doesn't enter.
unlink: slow=dummy, slow.next=1, slow.next.next=null. Now dummy.next = null.
return dummy.next → []

examples.note: Two-node list, remove the head — exercises the dummy with a slightly longer chain.
examples.trace:
dummy → 1 → 2
init: fast=dummy, slow=dummy
phase 1 (advance fast n=2 times):
  fast: dummy → 1 → 2
phase 2 (advance both until fast.next is null):
  fast=2, fast.next=null → loop doesn't enter.
unlink: slow=dummy, slow.next=1, slow.next.next=2. Now dummy.next = 2.
return dummy.next → [2]

sections.why: Tracing surfaces the two off-by-ones this problem is famous for. (1) The first-loop count — if you advance fast n-1 times instead of n, slow lands on the target rather than the predecessor, and you'd unlink the wrong node. (2) The second-loop condition — if you write `while (fast)` instead of `while (fast.next)`, slow walks one too far and again lands on the target. The [1], n=1 trace is the cleanest test of the dummy-head logic; without the dummy, you'd have to special-case 'returning null when the head is removed'.

sections.title: 5. Edge cases to mention
sections.prompt: What inputs would trip up a careless implementation?
sections.say:
"Before I declare it done, let me think about edges:
• Remove the head (n = L) → dummy handles it without a special case; slow ends at dummy, dummy.next gets reassigned.
• Remove the tail (n = 1) → fast advances 1 step in phase 1, then phase 2 walks until fast.next is null. slow ends at the second-to-last node.
• Single-node list with n = 1 → see the trace above; returns empty.
• n equals list length exactly (head removal) → handled.
• What I'm assuming and would want to confirm: n is valid (1 ≤ n ≤ L). If n > L, after phase 1 `fast` would be null and `fast.next` in phase 2 would throw. If n could exceed L, I'd add a length-check pass — but that defeats the single-pass goal, so usually the constraint is `n ≤ L`.
• Very long list (millions of nodes) → still O(L) time, O(1) space; no recursion stack issues."
sections.why: The 'remove the head' case is the one that JUSTIFIES the dummy — without that case being possible, the dummy is overkill. The 'n > L' note is the senior reflex — every two-pointer problem with a gap requires the gap to fit in the data, and flagging the assumption shows you've thought about the contract. Even if the constraints rule it out, naming it gives the interviewer the cue to confirm.

sections.title: 6. Complexity & wrap-up
sections.prompt: How would you defend the complexity claim?
sections.say:
"Time is O(L) where L is the list length. Phase 1 walks fast n steps. Phase 2 walks both pointers L - n more steps until fast.next is null. Total node-visits: n + (L - n) = L. One pass.

Space is O(1) — two pointer variables, plus the dummy node. No auxiliary structures.

If you wanted to extend to 'remove all nodes whose value equals X' (LeetCode 203), the dummy-head pattern carries over but the two-pointer dance becomes a single walk with a 'prev' pointer that only advances when not deleting. And 'find the n-th node from the end' (without removing it) is the same gap-of-n setup but you return slow.next instead of unlinking — same primitive, less work."
sections.why: The 'n + (L - n) = L' arithmetic is the clean defense of single-pass — it makes explicit that the two phases together visit each node at most once. The Remove Linked List Elements and 'find n-th from end' extensions prove you see the gap-pointer trick as a primitive rather than this problem's solution. That's how it shows up across the linked-list family — Middle of Linked List, Rotate List, Split Linked List in Parts all use variants of 'maintain a gap of K between two pointers'.

walkthrough.intro: Step through the single-pass two-pointer removal. Input is { values, n }. Watch fast race ahead by n, then slow + fast advance together — when fast.next is null, slow sits one before the target.
trace: const toList = (arr) => { const d = { val: 0, next: null }; let c = d; for (const v of arr) { c.next = { val: v, next: null }; c = c.next; } return d.next; };
const toArr = (h) => { const o = []; while (h) { o.push(h.val); h = h.next; } return o; };
yield { line: 1, label: `enter function — values=${JSON.stringify(values)}, n=${n}`, state: { values, n } };
yield { line: 2, label: 'create dummy → head (so removing head is not special)', state: { list: toArr(dummy.next), n } };
yield { line: 3, label: 'init fast=dummy, slow=dummy', state: { list: toArr(dummy.next), fastVal: 'dummy', slowVal: 'dummy', n } };
yield { line: 4, label: `fast +1 (step ${i + 1}/${n}) → ${fast ? fast.val : 'null'}`, state: { list: toArr(dummy.next), fastVal: fast ? fast.val : 'null', slowVal: 'dummy', n } };
yield { line: 4, label: `gap established — fast leads slow by ${n}`, state: { list: toArr(dummy.next), fastVal: fast ? fast.val : 'null', slowVal: 'dummy' } };
yield { line: 5, label: `advance both (iter ${iter}) — fast=${fast.val}, slow=${slow.val}`, state: { list: toArr(dummy.next), fastVal: fast.val, slowVal: slow.val } };

yield { line: 5, label: `loop exit — fast.next=null, slow sits BEFORE target ${slow.next ? slow.next.val : 'null'}`, state: { list: toArr(dummy.next), slowVal: slow.val, target: slow.next ? slow.next.val : 'null' } };
yield { line: 6, label: 'unlink: slow.next = slow.next.next', state: { list: toArr(dummy.next) } };
yield { line: 7, label: 'return dummy.next (skips the sentinel)', state: { list: toArr(dummy.next), returns: JSON.stringify(toArr(dummy.next)) } };

reference.approach: Gap-of-n two pointers, single pass, with a dummy head
notes: The dummy lets you remove the original head without a special case.
Walk fast n steps first, then advance both until fast.next is null — slow ends up at the predecessor of the target.
Stop the second loop on fast.next (not fast) so slow lands one before the removal target.
reference.crux: Open a gap of n between two pointers, then slide both until fast hits the end — slow lands on the target's predecessor; a dummy head makes removing the head non-special.
cruxDistractors: First pass to count length L, second pass to walk L−n steps to the predecessor, then unlink — correct, but two passes.
Open a gap of n−1 between the pointers so slow lands directly on the node to delete, then null it out.
Push all nodes onto a stack, pop n times to reach the target, and relink its predecessor — O(n) extra space.

alternates.label: Two-pass (count length, then walk)
alternates.when: Reach for this when clarity matters more than a single-pass constraint, or when the interviewer hasn't asked for one-pass. It's easier to get right on a whiteboard because there's no gap-pointer math — just count, compute L−n, walk, unlink.
notes: Two passes, same O(L) time as the one-pass version — just 2× the constant, not asymptotically worse.
The dummy node is still needed for the same reason: removing the head (n = L) means `steps = 0`, so `prev` stays at dummy and `dummy.next` gets reassigned.
No gap-pointer math: `len - n` gives the 0-indexed position of the predecessor from the dummy.

options: So fast and slow can start one node apart, establishing the n-gap implicitly
So removing the head node is not a special case
To turn the singly-linked list into a doubly-linked one for backward traversal
Because `slow.next.next` would deref null without an extra leading node
questions.explain: When n equals the list length, slow never leaves the dummy, so `slow.next = slow.next.next` drops the original head with the exact same line that drops any interior node — and `return dummy.next` hands back the correct new head, including null.

questions.q: After advancing fast n steps, why advance both until fast.next is null (not fast itself)?
options: Stopping on `fast` itself would skip the final node and leave slow one short of the predecessor
So slow lands on the node BEFORE the one to remove
`while (fast)` is fine — both conditions land slow on the same node
It prevents slow from walking past the tail and dereferencing null
questions.explain: Stopping when fast sits ON the tail leaves slow one before the target, which is what `slow.next = slow.next.next` needs; `while (fast)` runs one extra step and lands slow on the target itself (node 4 for [1,2,3,4,5], n=2).
Phase 1 walks fast n steps, phase 2 walks both L − n more: n + (L − n) = L node visits, one pass with no nested loop. O(n) is the wrong variable — n is the offset, not the input size.

questions.q: How is the actual unlink performed?
questions.explain: Skip the target by routing slow.next past it.
